title: Microplastics in seafood: size, sources, gut removal, bivalves eaten whole, FAO risk view and lost fishing gear

sources.title: Microplastics in fisheries and aquaculture (Fisheries and Aquaculture Technical Paper 615, 2017)
Fishing nets: the double-edged plastic swords in our ocean

facts.text: Microplastics are plastic pieces smaller than five millimeters.
A five-millimeter piece is about the size of a pencil eraser.
Some microplastics, such as microbeads once used in cleansers, are made small on purpose.
Many microplastics come from larger plastic items breaking down into smaller pieces.
Sea animals can mistake microplastics for food and swallow them.
In exposed fish, most microplastics are found in the digestive tract.
The gut of most seafood is removed before eating, which lowers exposure.
Bivalves such as mussels and oysters are usually eaten whole.
FAO judged the health risk from microplastics in seafood to be low with current knowledge.
FAO says the risk should be weighed against the health benefits of eating seafood.
Much about the smallest particles (nanoplastics) is still unknown; more research is needed.
Fishing gear lost at sea can keep catching fish for months or even years.
Most fishing gear is lost by accident, for example in storms or strong currents.
Nets left in the ocean can break down into microplastic pieces.
FAO supports low- or no-cost port facilities where fishers can hand in old or recovered gear.
